definition: Generative lexicon (GL) is a theory of linguistic semantics which focuses on the distributed nature of compositionality in natural language.
details: The first major work outlining the framework is James Pustejovsky's 1991 article "The Generative Lexicon". Subsequent important developments are presented in Pustejovsky and Boguraev (1993), Bouillon (1997), and Busa (1996). The first unified treatment of GL was given in Pustejovsky (1995). Unlike purely verb-based approaches to compositionality, generative lexicon attempts to spread the semantic load across all constituents of the utterance. Central to the philosophical perspective of GL are two major lines of inquiry: (1) How is it that we are able to deploy a finite number of words in our language in an unbounded number of contexts? (2) Is lexical information and the representations used in composing meanings separable from our commonsense knowledge?

explainer.lead: Generative lexicon is a theory of how words combine to produce meaning in natural language. It matters because a finite vocabulary can be used in endlessly many contexts, so word meanings must contribute flexibly rather than acting as fixed labels.

tiers.eli5: Think of words as pieces that each carry clues, not as a sentence where one word does all the work. When you put the pieces together, their clues help explain what the whole phrase means. This helps explain how the same words can make sense in many different situations.
tiers.practitioner: Generative lexicon is a linguistic semantics framework rather than a software tool. It is useful when reasoning about lexical representation and compositionality, especially when a verb-only account leaves too much meaning unexplained. A key pitfall is treating it as a ready-made implementation or assuming lexical meaning can always be separated from commonsense knowledge.
tiers.paperLevel: Generative lexicon is a theory of linguistic semantics in which compositionality is distributed across the constituents of an utterance rather than concentrated in the verb. James Pustejovsky introduced the framework in the 1991 article "The Generative Lexicon," with a unified treatment in Pustejovsky (1995). Its central open questions concern the unbounded contextual use of a finite vocabulary and whether lexical representations are separable from commonsense knowledge.

explainer.example: In "open the door," a generative-lexicon analysis does not assign the entire work of composing the meaning to "open." Both "open" and "the door" contribute to the interpretation, illustrating the framework's distribution of semantic load across constituents.

usedIn.detail: Provides a framework for studying how meanings are composed in utterances.

usedIn.name: Lexical semantics
usedIn.detail: Examines what information words carry and how that information supports different contexts of use.

usedIn.name: Compositionality research
usedIn.detail: Offers an alternative to approaches that place the semantic load primarily on verbs.

explainer.intuition: A sentence's meaning is not assembled by one central word with the other words merely filling slots. Generative lexicon spreads the work of composing meaning across all constituents.
howItWorks: Start with the finite set of words available in a language.
Treat each constituent as contributing information to the utterance's meaning.
Combine those contributions rather than deriving composition solely from the verb.
Use the resulting account to examine how words can appear in an unbounded range of contexts.
Consider whether this lexical information can be separated from commonsense knowledge.
explainer.whyItMatters: It addresses a basic puzzle of language: people can use a limited vocabulary successfully in limitless contexts. It also puts the relationship between lexical meaning and commonsense knowledge at the center of semantic theory.
misconceptions: It is not a purely verb-based theory of compositionality.
It does not claim that lexical information is necessarily independent of commonsense knowledge; that separability is one of its central questions.
It is a theory of linguistic semantics, not a named software system.
